```console
$ measure `len(json.dumps(Server(repo).handle(tools/list)["result"]["tools"]))`; then `uv run pytest tests/test_mcp_tool_budget.py tests/test_mcp_tool_tiers.py -q`
tools/list = 97,394 bytes; budget 100,000 -> 2,606 bytes of headroom (was 6). 15 passed in 2.85s, both files that read the constant.
```

## Across the whole open roadmap (about 700 tasks, 70 phases), which tasks must depend on each other, which can share one engine, and which cross-cutting gaps are missing?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Analysis of the task graph found (1) 233 body references to other tasks without a dependency edge, of which about 35 are real extends or reuses; (2) nine engines planned piecemeal in many phases where one shared engine is cheaper: person-only approvals (17 phases), waivers (5 places), record kinds (about 15 new kinds all hand-written), event kinds (73 tasks), the MCP tool-list budget (241 tasks touch MCP), seeded evaluation fixtures (31 phases, 12+ separate eval tasks), sensitivity and confidentiality handling (6 places), shipped workflow packs (7 phases ship template data), and actor identity and roles (3 auth models); (3) hot files (README.md, config.py, mcp.py, events.py, model.py) that about 9,000 cross-phase task pairs would contend for, while the new phases declare no globs yet.
- **Mechanism.** A script over the task graph: transitive dependency closure, glob overlap, body-reference scan and keyword census per engine. The fixes are a shared-engines phase with edges from every consumer, missing dependency edges, and priority lifting of prerequisites.
- **Falsifier.** If the shared engines are built and a consumer still needs its own copy, or the new edges create a cycle or stall a ready chain, the review is wrong.

**Probe:**

```console
$ graph scripts over the 718 open tasks; no cycles after the edits; see the commit
```

**Sources:** the open task graph (ddflow list/show), this session's phase filings

## How easily can ddflow be integrated with, and managed remotely through, Paseo, AgentOS, Harness Remote, Nimbalyst, Orca, Emdash and comparable control planes, and which features does it still lack?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** Every plane can consume ddflow as an MCP server today (with a lean tool profile) and most can receive notifications; the real conflict is worktree and session ownership, because Paseo, AgentOS, Orca, Emdash and Nimbalyst each create their own worktrees. So ddflow needs adopt-claims for foreign worktrees, foreign ids in the lane ledger, a pluggable lane-backend interface (paseo-cli, opencode-http, tmux, orca-cli, acp), an ACP proxy that claims an item and injects the ddflow MCP server and cwd, an attention-items API, a push feed with idempotency keys, scoped tokens and transfer-pack renderers. Paseo is the best fit; its plugin is the hardest and last piece.
- **Mechanism.** Built on ddflow serve, auth, events and ask (P-remote), the lane launcher and descriptors (P-agent-parity), spawn and notify (P-spawn), the lane ledger, transfer packs and the typed registry; new pieces are the adopt-claim, foreign ids, the backend interface and its backends, the ACP wrapper, attention items, push feed, scoped tokens, renderers and a conflict doctor.
- **Falsifier.** If a stub control plane cannot start a lane, see its events and approve an attention item, or ddflow deletes an adopted worktree, or two tools claim one worktree without a reported conflict, the design fails.

**Sources:** https://paseo.sh/ and docs (SDK @getpaseo/client, CLI, plugins, ACP provider), https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os, https://github.com/monperrus/harness-remote, https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst, https://github.com/stablyai/orca, https://www.onorca.dev/docs/cli/reference, https://github.com/generalaction/emdash, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control, https://agentclientprotocol.com/overview/introduction, https://zed.dev/docs/ai/external-agents, https://opencode.ai/docs/server/

## How far can ddflow manage a project itself (propose next features, optimise, correct old code, build from user stories and goals) and act as architect and product manager, with the operator keeping authority?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** Agents succeed on well-scoped work with a machine-checkable oracle and fail at project level through verifier hacking (the Darwin Gödel Machine removed its own hallucination markers; instructions barely reduce reward hacking), spec and handoff errors, drift and cost. So autonomy must be a per-class ladder (suggest, prepare, execute with approval, execute within budget) that only the operator raises, the oracle files and gate config must be outside the agent's write scope, every proposal needs evidence and a kill criterion, and the narrow execute-within-budget classes come last.
- **Mechanism.** Proposals are a record kind with person-only adoption; scheduled observation jobs file them; architect and product-manager workflows are template data over decisions, goals, research and the gate pipeline; fitness functions turn architecture drivers into gates; a calibration loop compares predicted with actual; a kill switch and automatic demotion bound the damage.
- **Falsifier.** If a seeded fixture lets an agent edit its own oracle or gate config, merge outside its class, adopt its own proposal, exceed its budget, or file a proposal with no evidence, the design fails.

**Sources:** https://cognition.ai (Devin annual review), https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954 (Darwin Gödel Machine), https://www.theregister.com (DGM cheating), https://metr.org (reward hacking), https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system, https://martinfowler.com (Böckeler on spec-driven development); SICA, MAST, GitClear, DORA, Copilot agent, Kiro, Spec Kit, BMAD seen as snippets

## How can projects in one organisation or division share lessons, decisions, rules, goals, policies, research, session summaries, subagents, companions, configuration and datasets through a remote knowledge base with its own protocol, without poisoning, leaking or overriding local project knowledge?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** A pull-and-propose protocol over immutable content-addressed records with separate signed attestations, a sequence-numbered NDJSON feed with opaque cursors, a scope tree as the only access unit, a local read-only mirror, propose-only agents and server-assigned trust gives selective sync, idempotent offline writes and auditable promotion; the knowledge feed stays advisory and only signed policy bundles that pin record digests can enforce, so the feed cannot carry tool grants, hooks or commands.
- **Mechanism.** DKP (wire id ddflow.kb/1): discover, pull, snapshot, get, search, propose, attest, retract, subscribe, ack; records enter a separate imported layer of the local fold and the local event log is never overwritten; a git mirror with an inbox directory is the first transport (pull request as proposal), the HTTP hub the second, an MCP read-only facade the third.
- **Falsifier.** If a seeded fixture lets an imported record carry a tool grant or command, overwrite a local project record, reach another scope's reader, survive a leak retraction, or be injected as an instruction without a pinned bundle, the design fails.

**Sources:** https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification (resources, authorization, elicitation), https://a2a-protocol.org (agent card), https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec (OCI referrers), https://electric-sql.com/docs/api/http (shape log, up-to-date/must-refetch), https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956 (Zep/Graphiti), https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413 (Mem0), https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ (read in full by the research agent; Copilot, Cursor, Cody, Claude Code managed settings seen as snippets)

## How can ddflow write and maintain requirements (project, vendor, code), vendor-relationship documents and product-management documents as a reviewed pipeline, safely with untrusted vendor material?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** LLM-written requirements read as correct but are less unambiguous and feasible and can contradict themselves (62% judged realistic in one study, yet contradictions on close reading), and LLM trace links are about 80% F1; so a requirement must carry a mandatory source, pass a deterministic lint before any model review, be accepted only by a person, and link through hash-based suspect links. Vendor documents are an untrusted channel (prompt injection; the lethal trifecta), so the reader of vendor material must have no send capability and the agent never sends, signs, accepts terms or spends.
- **Mechanism.** Structured things (requirement, stakeholder, vendor, contract, risk, assumption, goal link) are definition-record kinds on the record contract; narrative documents (PRD, RFP/SOW pack, vendor profile, roadmap, release notes) are document types whose regions are generated from the records; lint rules are data on the docs-check engine; trace links hash their parent; vendor material is stored by reference and hash with trust=external; reading is split from planning by the capability envelope; dates are computed in code.
- **Falsifier.** If a seeded fixture passes the pipeline with an invented requirement (no source), an ambiguous or non-singular requirement, a contradiction, a hallucinated standard, a vendor document carrying an injected instruction that is obeyed, a wrong notice deadline or a synthesis with no verbatim quotes, the design fails.

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.10886 (29148 + LLM check, snippet), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.08847 (requirements smells), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easy_Approach_to_Requirements_Syntax, https://docs.rtems.org/docs/6.2/eng/req/tooling.html (Doorstop suspect links, snippet), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.09335 (300 synthetic specs, snippet), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.03256 (MARE, snippet), https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/feature-specs/requirements-first/, https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/, https://today.ucsd.edu/story/how-much-does-chatbot-bias-influence-users-a-lot-it-turns-out

## How should ddflow run, generate, maintain and record tests of every kind (unit to chaos, hardware, UI, deployment, CI/CD, load, mutation, scientific), with tests written as Markdown unless the user says otherwise, inside a big job or in a repo that only holds tests?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** Agent-written tests are only as good as the oracle and the filters around them: fail-before/pass-after proof, mutation score instead of coverage, repeated runs, read-only tests for the implementer, an independent author, and an explicit unavailable for absent benches and tools. Markdown test cards that an agent runs and records as observations, promoted to code once stable, fit the repo and the review flow; each kind of test is a data row (runner, oracle, cadence, stop rule), not new machinery.
- **Mechanism.** A test-kind registry generates per-kind gate pipelines on the existing machinery; results are run records with SUT pin, repeats and seed; test cards are a document type (the scenario card extended); quality is checked by mutation, flake ledger and a test review lens; traceability reuses claims and their executable checks; cadence reuses scheduled jobs and the promotion pipeline.
- **Falsifier.** If a seeded fixture of bad tests (asserts the bug, tautology, deleted test, updated snapshot, flaky, mock-only) passes the shipped workflows, or a test-only repository cannot record which SUT version a result is for, the design fails.

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12952 (SWT-Bench), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.09171 (Meta TestGen-LLM), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.12862 (Meta ACH), https://www.anthropic.com/research/property-based-testing, https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qJYMbrabcQqCZ7iqm/impossiblebench-measuring-reward-hacking-in-llm-coding-1, https://playwright.dev/docs/test-agents, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.00409 (over-mocking, snippet), https://engineering.fb.com/2018/11/21/developer-tools/predictive-test-selection/

## How should ddflow run research of any kind (architecture, math, hardware, DSP, science, ML), standalone or as a phase of development, so it converges on a best answer and the result is recorded and reusable?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** Systems whose every proposal passes an automated verifier (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, autoresearch) produce real results; LLM-judgement-only systems fabricate (AI Scientist v1: 42% of experiments crashed, 57% of manuscripts had wrong numbers). So ddflow should require a named verifier, a committed pre-registered plan, prediction-before-observation, a stop rule and budget, a mechanical citation and number audit, and a confidence ladder, expressed as DATA over engines it already has or has planned.
- **Mechanism.** A research workflow template (stages, verifier, stop rules, budget, roles, rules, output records) drives the existing per-kind gate pipeline (kind_pipelines.research) with command/agent gates; hypotheses, predictions, observations and ruled-out results are reasoning-log steps; evidence is claims with sources and grades; plans are a document type with a sha stamp; runs are job/scenario records; the skeptic is a cross-family review lens; re-verification is a watch; reuse is the record-contract context and RAG export.
- **Falsifier.** If a seeded fixture with planted traps (a dead citation, a confirming-only test, a number not tied to a run, a forking path) passes the pipeline, or if a standalone research item cannot be completed without a code-style worktree, the design is wrong.

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131 (AlphaEvolve), https://deepmind.google/blog/co-scientist-a-multi-agent-ai-partner-to-accelerate-research/, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14297 (AI Scientist evaluation), https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.01507 (forking paths, snippet only), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_competing_hypotheses, https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14207 (STORM)

## How does ddflow share context between sessions and agents, locally and remotely, and push a change from the master, a rule, a decision or the user into sessions that are already working?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** The plan covers three things well: record changes reaching a running session through the doors its harness calls (B-rc-changes, B-rc-context), hand-off and fork between sessions and harnesses (B-sc-transfer), and the session tree and native lane status; it does not cover directed, live context: a message from the master or the user to a lane or a scope with urgency and acknowledgement, impact analysis of a change on the lanes that are working, a staleness marker for what a lane was told, peer-to-peer sharing between lanes, or context for remote and cloud sessions that cannot read local files
- **Mechanism.** event log with lamport marks and per-session cursors; doors a harness calls (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and tool hooks with additionalContext where they exist, MCP replies, heartbeat and wait elsewhere); handoff records (session.handoff) and fenced transfers (session.transferred); D-session-context bars ddflow from calling the remote-session tools of the host; harness-native message routes exist (Kilo prompt_async queues while busy, Claude SendMessage, Codex message to an agent thread, Cursor queued messages) and P-spawn.steer plans to use them for children only; remote and cloud agents see the repository and MCP/HTTP, not .ddflow/local
- **Falsifier.** a command or event already addresses a message to a running lane, or tells which lanes a changed rule affects, or serves a pack to a cloud session

**Probe:**

```console
$ inventory: B-rc-changes, B-rc-context, B-sc-transfer, B-sc-tree, B-sc-native-status, B-am-restart-brief, D-session-context, P-spawn, P-remote, P-multiuser; the agent reports for mid-session injection rungs
B-rc-changes: one change feed, per-session cursor, delivered at doors, relevant_to filter, record kinds only; B-sc-transfer: addressed fenced hand-off pack, fork; B-sc-tree: parent/role/goal fields; no task addresses a free-text directive to a lane, computes which running lanes a rule or safeguard edit affects, marks a lane's context stale, records acknowledgement, shares notes between peers, or serves packs to remote sessions; others (general knowledge, not surveyed): Claude Code agent teams message teammates, Kilo/opencode prompt_async queues, Codex messages to agents, Cursor queued messages, VS Code handoffs, ACP prompt and cancel, the A2A protocol, blackboard and publish-subscribe designs
```

## Does opencode 1.19.0 really block the parent session while a subagent runs, and which routes free it?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** In opencode 1.19.0 the task tool runs the subagent as a child session and the parent stays busy until the child finishes (blocking); the documented detach route did not free it in this setup; aborting the child does free the parent immediately
- **Mechanism.** task tool creates a child session observable at GET /session/{id}/children; /session/status shows the parent busy for the child's whole run; POST /experimental/session/{id}/background is documented to detach blocking subagents; POST /session/{child}/abort stops the child
- **Falsifier.** the parent goes idle while the child still runs, or the detach route frees the parent

**Probe:**

```console
$ opencode-ai 1.19.0 in a scratch directory with isolated HOME; opencode serve --pure; free anonymous model opencode/big-pickle (no credential); a parent session prompted via prompt_async to use the task tool once for a subagent running 'sleep 35'; polled /session/status and /session/{id}/children every 2 s; run 1 called POST /experimental/session/{id}/background 8 s after the child appeared; run 2 called POST /session/{child}/abort; run 3 called POST /api/session/{parent}/interrupt
run 1: child session appeared at 6 s, parent stayed busy from 2 s to 44 s, detach call at 14 s returned (200, false) and changed nothing, parent went idle at 46 s right after the child finished, final assistant text FINISHED; run 2: abort of the child returned (200, true) and both parent and child were idle within 2 s (the parent's turn ended too); run 3: INCONCLUSIVE (the model never started a child in that run, so interrupt was not exercised); my sleep-process counter was unreliable (it counted its own pgrep) and is discarded; free models listed without credentials: opencode/big-pickle, nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, ling-3.1-flash-free and others; Kilo not probed model-backed (installed 7.2.20 too old)
```

## Can ddflow run periodic and event-triggered work per project, fully managed by the user, for full-suite checks (duplication, bugs, security), dependency and partner-tool updates, and for ddflow itself keeping up with the coding agents?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** The definitions and the trigger engine exist; what is missing is the user-facing management, the calendar and watch evaluation, an executor that works the queue unattended, and a generic way to watch upstream tools, so today only count-based cadence passes (integration tests, dedupe sweep, architecture review, mutation tests, lessons) actually come due; the rest is planned in P-schedule but blocked behind the docs wave, and keeping up with agent updates and partner tools has no generic mechanism
- **Mechanism.** shipped: job definitions in the log, .ddflow/schedules/*.toml or [cadence] with validation (schedule.defined/updated/removed), event triggers in .ddflow/triggers/*.toml with window, debounce, cooldown, dedupe key, hop limit, breaker and a global cap, firing creates a queue item from a job template and never starts an agent (D-trigger-actions-create-items), and ddflow cadence for count passes; D-sched-no-daemon means due-ness is computed from the log and something else must start it; planned and open: B-sched-due (calendar due), B-sched-run (run a due job, file items), B-sched-author (CLI and one MCP tool), B-sched-emitters (cron, systemd, Actions snippets and a doctor warning for a silent no-fire), B-sched-defaults (security, dependency, architecture, duplication, CI-health jobs), B-trigger-events and B-trigger-defaults, B-sched-escalation
- **Falsifier.** a command already lists, edits and runs scheduled jobs, or an existing mechanism watches upstream versions and changelogs

**Probe:**

```console
$ ddflow schedule (no such command), ddflow cadence output, README Cadences, Scheduled jobs and Event triggers sections, open P-schedule tasks and their bodies, ddflow --help command list, search for watch, upstream and release-check work
ddflow has no schedule or trigger command (ddflow --help lists cadence only); ddflow cadence shows only DUE integration_tests and dedupe_sweep by task count (749 tasks since last); calendar every_days jobs are defined but nothing evaluates them (B-sched-due open); no task starts an agent to work the queue unattended (the launcher is P-agent-parity.launcher); the only upstream watch is ddflow's own release check (B-upgrade.8, done) and bespoke planned checks (P-agent-parity.drift, companions listing); P-schedule is 4/16 and waits for the docs wave
```

## How can ddflow observe itself and each project's workflow, with the help of the LLM and the agents, find defects, inefficiency and deviations, propose improvements at the right moments, and optimise itself safely?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** ddflow already holds the raw material (an event log with case ids, states, agents and timestamps, plus doctor notes, gate rates, flake detection, cadence misses, the adaptive flow controller and a planned metrics service) and the delivery channels (jobs, triggers, a proposal record in P-goals, change feeds), but nothing joins them into detect, interpret, propose, apply and measure: detection is scattered notes with no finding record, no LLM retrospective with verification exists, proposals are not typed or applicable, there are no phase-boundary moments, and no bounded experiment loop; the log is a process-mining event log, so conformance and bottleneck analysis can be deterministic, with the LLM used for interpretation and proposals that must cite evidence and survive a cross-family check
- **Mechanism.** events carry item, state change, agent and time; gate.* events give yield and duration; lease and claim events give lock waits (claim refusals are NOT logged today); doctor emits ad hoc notes (gate_flapping, duplicate_work, cadence behind, flaky test, orphan worktrees); services/rates.py measures gate fire rates and cadence hit rates; flowstate samples signals for the AIMD controller; B-prop-model/B-prop-discover plan a proposal record and a periodic discovery job; schedule jobs and triggers create items; lessons, decisions and rules are the memory an analysis needs
- **Falsifier.** the existing log cannot answer where time goes per item (state durations, rework, waits), or a cross-family model's improvement proposals cannot be checked against the log

**Probe:**

```console
$ inventory: doctor note kinds, services/rates.py, flowstate/flowcontrol, ddflow loops, cadence passes, the open tasks of P-goals (B-prop-*, B-goal-report, B-goal-eval), P-schedule (B-sched-run, B-trigger-*), P-gaps (B-gap-metrics), P-lessons, P-governor, P-change-surface.footprint; doctor on this repo; forced-completion repair found 12 deviations from the defined pipeline at upgrade
doctor note kinds seen: gate_flapping (13), duplicate_work (3), cadence behind (2), flaky test (1), orphan_worktree (59), embedder; the upgrade repair found 12 items completed with --force over unmet gates, i.e. conformance checking against the defined pipeline already finds real deviations; no finding record, no claim.refused event, no phase.started/research.completed trigger source, no typed proposal, no experiment loop; B-prop-model (proposal record, person-only adopt/defer/reject), B-prop-discover (disabled-by-default periodic discovery) and B-goal-report (acceptance rate) are open; others (from general knowledge, not freshly surveyed): process mining and conformance checking on event logs, DORA and flow metrics (cycle time, WIP, throughput), SRE postmortems and error budgets, Kaizen retrospectives, AIOps anomaly detection, LLM self-improvement research (Reflexion, Voyager skill library, Agent Workflow Memory, DSPy and TextGrad prompt optimisation, self-modifying agents), and their known failure modes (Goodhart, LLM-as-judge self-preference, feedback loops)
```

## Why is the opencode adapter gated to v1, and what changes with v2?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** The gate is on the PLUGIN only: the v2 (dev) build serves the same HTTP session API as 1.19.0, so server-driven spawn, steer, abort, wait and detach work on both, while the plugin API changed incompatibly, so the continuation and monitoring plugin needs a second implementation
- **Mechanism.** npm dist-tags: latest 1.19.0, dev 0.0.0-dev-202610110139, next 0.0.0-next-202606270058, beta 0.0.0-beta-202608110357; source reading (group 2 report): v1 plugin is @opencode-ai/plugin with named hooks (chat.message, tool.execute.before/after, event, experimental.session.compacting); v2 is @opencode/plugin with Plugin.define({id, setup(ctx)}) and hooks namespaced under ctx.session.hook(...)
- **Falsifier.** the dev build lacks a session route the v1 server has, or its plugin still loads a v1 plugin unchanged

**Probe:**

```console
$ installed opencode-ai@dev into a scratch dir (isolated HOME), served it on [REDACTED:ipv4], compared /doc paths with 1.19.0; npm view opencode-ai dist-tags
dev build 0.0.0-dev-202610110139 serves 162 paths, the same count as 1.19.0, including GET /session/status, GET /session/{id}/children, POST /session/{id}/prompt_async, POST /session/{id}/abort, POST /api/session/{id}/interrupt, POST /api/session/{id}/wait, GET /api/session/active, POST /experimental/session/{id}/background; npm latest is still 1.19.0; the plugin API difference is from source reading, NOT probed in the binary (no plugin was loaded)
```

## How do subagents, parallel sessions and steering behave in opencode 1.19.0, probed on the real binary?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** opencode runs subagents SYNCHRONOUSLY by default, which blocks the parent session (the behaviour the operator saw on Kilo, the same engine family), and its own server API offers the escape: a child-session tree, an experimental route that detaches blocking subagents into the background, abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async and parallel sessions under one server
- **Mechanism.** opencode serve exposes two API surfaces: the legacy /session routes and a newer /api/session routes; subagents are child sessions of the parent (GET /session/{id}/children); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background is documented as 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'
- **Falsifier.** the background route or the children route is absent in 1.19.0, or two sessions cannot exist at once under one server

**Probe:**

```console
$ npm install [REDACTED:email] into a scratch directory with an isolated HOME and XDG dirs; opencode --help; opencode serve --port 47811 --pure; curl /session, POST /session twice, POST /session/{id}/abort, GET /doc and read the operation descriptions; the same on the installed Kilo 7.2.20
opencode 1.19.0 installed and running; commands include acp (Agent Client Protocol server), serve, attach <url>, run, session, export/import, plugin, db, --pure (no external plugins); two parallel sessions created under one server; abort on an idle session returned true [200]; /doc lists 162 paths: legacy GET,POST /session, GET /session/status, GET /session/{id}/children, POST /session/{id}/prompt_async ('returning immediately'), POST /session/{id}/abort, /fork, /summarize, /command, /shell, /diff, /permissions; new /api/session/{id}/wait ('Wait for a session agent loop to become idle'), /interrupt, /prompt, /model, /agent, /compact, /permission, /question, GET /api/session/active ('foreground Session drains owned by this process'); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background = 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'. Kilo 7.2.20 (installed, several releases behind 7.8.8) serves a 7-path /doc, so the same routes are NOT confirmed for Kilo. Not probed: a model-backed run (no provider credentials were used), so the blocking is read from the schema, not observed in a live task
```

## How should the master session delegate work to subagents or spawned agents in every coding agent without blocking, pass data and context to them, and stay free to research, spawn more and correct running tasks?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** A master stays free only if delegation returns at once and results come back as notices, not as a tool return; every agent offers one of three routes: a native background subagent (Claude run_in_background and background frontmatter, Grok spawn_subagent default run_in_background, Cursor and Antigravity background agents), an independent session driven by a process or server (kilo serve with prompt_async and an abort endpoint, kilo run -s, codex exec resume, opencode run, gemini -p, cline --id), or a manual brief; a blocking subagent tool (the Kilo behaviour the operator observed) is the wrong route for long work; ddflow has the pieces (lane launcher plan, lanes ledger, dispatch brief, hand-off pack, change feed) but nothing chooses the route, returns at once, notifies the master, steers a running lane or defines what context crosses
- **Mechanism.** agent reports of 2026-10-12: Claude Agent tool run_in_background plus SendMessage to continue and a 10-minute background idle cap in -p; Grok spawn_subagent run_in_background default true, isolation worktree, resume_from, depth 1; Codex spawn_agent with message, task_name, model and reasoning_effort; Kilo prompt_async queues a prompt while busy, POST /session/:id/abort stops, GET /event streams, sessions run in parallel under one server; Cursor cloud agents and the & prefix; Antigravity 2.0 parallel agents; Gemini subagents are static definitions; ddflow job run already detaches a process; the change feed of P-record-contract and the lanes ledger can carry the notices
- **Falsifier.** a harness has no way to run work outside the master's turn, or the master cannot be told a lane finished without polling

**Probe:**

```console
$ scan of the four agent reports and the remote-management report for async, background, steer, resume and abort facts; ddflow search and task lists for spawn, steer, lane and hand-off work in P-agent-parity, P-remote, P-session-context, P-safeguards and B-gap-lanes
Claude: run_in_background, SendMessage, background frontmatter, -p background wait ceiling 10 min; Grok: run_in_background default true, resume_from, depth 1; Codex: spawn_agent task_name/message, no verified background semantics; Kilo: prompt_async queue-while-busy, abort, parallel sessions, Task-tool blocking UNVERIFIED (operator-observed); Gemini: static subagents, blocking unknown; Cursor/Antigravity/Copilot cloud: background agents; queue: lane launcher (start/stop/resume/steer verbs), lanes ledger (done), dispatch brief, B-sc-transfer, B-rc-changes, P-remote.launch (steer) all open, no route chooser, no notify-the-master task, no steer semantics, no definition of what context crosses
```

## Are lessons learned used well enough to prevent repeated mistakes, drift and other issues, and is the lessons interface properly developed?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Lessons are recorded but barely wired in: 72 lessons exist against 513 fixed bugs and about 1,200 tasks, 1 of 72 has a self-check pattern and 1 has globs, so delivery is by text ranking in the brief only; nothing is delivered by glob at claim or into a subagent's brief, nothing records delivery or recurrence, there is no edit, retire or merge verb, no promotion of a recurring lesson into a check or safeguard, and the lessons cadence pass was overdue and skipped; the interface is complete only for add, list, search and verify
- **Mechanism.** ddflow lesson has add, verify, search, list (MCP: add, search, verify); lesson.recorded is the only lesson event kind; brief ranks lessons against the task text (lessons.max_results 5); lessons carry rule/why/how/tags/seen_in but patterns and globs are optional and almost never set; seen_in is hand-written; the open BL-knowledge tasks (B197 recurrence, B199 correct and retire, B202 pins, B204 recall before implementing) have waited since 2026-09-28 behind the docs wave
- **Falsifier.** lessons are scoped (globs or patterns) in most cases, or a recurrence count exists and shows lessons working

**Probe:**

```console
$ count lesson.recorded events and their fields in .ddflow/events; ddflow lesson verify; ddflow lesson --help; ddflow config --explain --filter lessons.; ddflow list task --phase BL-knowledge; ddflow cadence

## How can ddflow put short, relevant coding-standard, style and API guidance in front of the agent while it writes, using companion MCP servers such as codeguide and context7, so produced code drifts less?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** The companions are bound to gates only (codeguide and context7 serve the standards and research gates), so they act at review time, after the drift; ddflow itself is an MCP server and not a client, so only the agent can call them; the exact style facts already live in the project's tool configs and the API facts in the pinned dependency versions, so short cards can be derived or cached and delivered at claim and dispatch, with the companion consulted by the agent when a card is missing
- **Mechanism.** ddflow companions: codeguide serves language and framework standards as MCP resources, context7 current library documentation; both are registered in the agent's MCP config, listed for gates standards and research; services/guidance injects ranked, budgeted, fenced text at brief and claim; lock files give exact versions; ruff/pyproject/eslint/prettier/editorconfig hold the enforceable style; hooks (post_tool) can see whether the agent called a companion tool on harnesses with that rung
- **Falsifier.** a companion call or a style/API card is already delivered to the agent before it edits, or the agent cannot be told reliably which companion call to make

**Probe:**

```console
$ ddflow companions output; services/companions.py gate bindings; grep for a consult/card action; the guidance injection path in brief and claim
codeguide: gates=[standards]; context7: gates=[research, standards]; no action, event or command makes an agent consult them before writing; guidance injection carries rule text only; ddflow has no MCP client code (only server)
```

## What does ddflow have and plan for managing subagents, skills and safeguards (inserted at session start, claim and dispatch), editable, reviewable and logged on CLI and MCP from shared code, and for cost and complexity?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Subagents (P-subagents, 14 tasks) and skills (P-skills, 13) have full lifecycle plans on the shared record surface, and rules are shipped with CRUD on CLI and MCP and are injected by glob at brief and claim; but a SAFEGUARD does not exist as a thing: a rule is text only (no trigger, audience or action), nothing records that a session or subagent actually RECEIVED a safeguard, the subagent dispatch path carries none, subagents and skills have no capability or cost envelope (allowed tools, paths, turn/token/spend caps), and there is no single view of what governs a session
- **Mechanism.** rule files hold id, title, tags, scope, priority, globs and text (.ddflow/rules/*.toml); brief and claim print the governing text ranked by globs; enforcement is hard-coded in services/enforce.py (commit and lease checks), approvals, reviewer trust and quotas; the implement driver tells a coordinator how to dispatch a subagent but nothing assembles or logs the subagent's brief; subagent and skill tasks need B-uni-record-surface and depend on the docs wave; cost lives in separate plans (B-gap-spend, B-sub-metrics, P-governor, B-skills-export-docs cost column)
- **Falsifier.** an event or command shows which safeguards a given session or subagent was handed, or a rule can express a refuse/cap action

**Probe:**

```console
$ ddflow rule show; .ddflow/rules/*.toml fields; grep core/defs.py for enforcement fields; ddflow search for delivered/safeguard/envelope; ddflow list task for P-subagents P-skills P-agent-rules B-rules-*; needs of B-sub-events B-skills-events B-sub-route B-sub-sod B-sub-trust
rule fields: id,title,tags,scope,priority,globs,created,updated,content only; no event kind records delivery of guidance; P-subagents: model, events, sync, route, sod, trust, metrics, eval, defaults, doctor, onboard, docs, decide, org-kinds; P-skills: model, events, author, sync, install, doctor, onboard, context, pack, mcp-serving, eval, export-docs, acceptance; B-sub-events/B-skills-events need B-uni-record-surface (the descriptor) but not the lifecycle of P-record-contract; enforcement checks are code in enforce.py, not data
```

## How big are ddflow's files in bytes and tokens, what share of the code sits in oversized files, and what would a 20 KB limit change for a model with a 128k context window?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Almost half the source bytes sit in 57 files over 20 KB (12 files over 50 KB hold 20%), and 43 test files exceed 20 KB; one change commonly needs several of them, so a 128k-context model cannot hold a typical change plus the instructions; a 20 KB limit (about 5k tokens a file) with packages of smaller modules makes a change fit, shrinks leases to the part being changed and shrinks the bug surface
- **Mechanism.** tokens are about bytes/4; lease conflicts are per file glob (importer vs importer refused claims this session); an LLM reads a whole file to edit part of it; the existing 600-line module guidance has 35 files over it (a line limit hides long lines: importer.py is 158 KB); tests, pins and docs are loaded by agents too (setup/ops transcript 440 KB, README 425 KB, two goldens 130-140 KB)
- **Falsifier.** a typical change touches files totalling under 40k tokens already, or oversized files are cohesive units that cannot be split without raising import fan-in and bugs

**Probe:**

```console
$ python scan of *.py under ddflow/ and tests/ (bytes, lines, share of total, median and p90) and of docs and pins over 100 KB; git history of merges (R-change-surface); import graph (396 modules)

Pins and docs over 100 KB: setup_ops transcript JSON 440 KB, README 425 KB, docs/ddflow/RESEARCH.md 327 KB, BACKLOG 158 KB, two golden .ambr 132-139 KB. A change like ddflow list touched 9 files; the 12 largest source files alone are 1.0 MB = ~250k tokens

## How can ddflow be started and managed remotely from OpenClaw and similar tools, and must ddflow start the coding agents itself?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** ddflow can be driven remotely today by the pull model (the remote tool starts agents that call ddflow's MCP, or runs the CLI over SSH); first-class remote management needs a stateless optional serve surface with real authentication and roles, a cursor-based event stream, approvals and questions as data, and run handles; ddflow starting agents is a second step that reuses the lane launcher (P-agent-parity.launcher) and must keep launch templates operator-only
- **Mechanism.** OpenClaw is a self-hosted gateway (MIT, many chat channels, cron and heartbeat, authenticated inbound hooks) that is an MCP server and client and drives coding agents over ACP (stdio) with approve-all/approve-reads/deny-all modes; Claude Remote Control attaches claude.ai to a local session over an outbound connection; n8n and Hermes are MCP clients. ddflow today has a hand-written stdio MCP server, a log with wait, jobs, ticks, leases, and no authentication (operator-only verbs hold by convention), and D-sched-no-daemon forbids a daemon, so any serve process must be optional, opt-in and stateless
- **Falsifier.** OpenClaw or another target cannot call a stdio MCP server or the CLI at all, or a remote-only approval round trip cannot be made safe without a trusted channel

**Probe:**

```console
$ one research report from primary docs and ddflow code, 2026-10-12 (web claims came through a summarising fetch tool: re-read before building); read of ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py, mcp_protocol.py, waits, jobs, ticks, approval and quota code
OpenClaw: 392k stars, releases several times a day, 20+ channels, openclaw mcp serve (stdio) and MCP client, ACP via acpx, inbound hooks /hooks/agent and /hooks/wake, one trust boundary per gateway, poor security record from press (secondary); ACP spec is stdio only, HTTP transport draft; n8n MCP server trigger speaks SSE and streamable HTTP, not stdio; ddflow: stdlib stdio MCP, legacy plus stateless 2026-07-28 protocols, [mcp-sdk] HTTP extra declared and unused, no authentication, quota/governor decided but not built, no agent is started by ddflow; claude -p without --bare runs project hooks and .mcp.json servers without a trust dialog (cloned-repo threat)
```

## Can ddflow behave the same on every coding agent, and what is missing to get there?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Parity is reachable for nearly every agent through a fallback ladder, but ddflow lacks four shared pieces: a continuation engine that decides stop-or-continue and emits each harness's mechanism, a ddflow-owned headless launcher, descriptor sections for detection, headless, continuation, meters and caps, and a behavioural parity suite; the descriptors also contain facts that the 2026-10-12 research shows are wrong
- **Mechanism.** Every agent but Cline, Aider, Zed, Replit, Jules and Cascade offers some stop-and-continue: Claude/Qwen/Goose/Junie/Droid/Devin CLI/Copilot/Antigravity/Grok via a Stop hook that blocks or continues (caps of 5-8), Cursor via the stop hook's followup_message, Amp via plugin agent.end, Kilo and opencode 1.x via a plugin whose session.idle handler calls client.session.promptAsync (probed on Kilo 7.2.20), Cline and the rest only by an external re-invocation (cline --id, aider --message, codex/gemini/grok headless resume). So the rung differs per agent but one decision function can drive all of them
- **Falsifier.** an agent with a documented hook or plugin API cannot continue a session after it stops, or the external re-invocation loses the session so continuity cannot be kept

**Probe:**

```console
$ four parallel research reports 2026-10-12 from primary docs and source trees (groups 1-4, reports in the scratchpad), a live Kilo 7.2.20 plugin probe, a Claude Code 2.1.296 stub-MCP handshake probe, and a read of ddflow's 22 harness descriptors, deltas and the queue (P-harness-adapters, P-agent-compat, P-agent-hygiene, P-agent-memory, B-hy-stop-protocol)
Kilo 7.2.20: a throw in tool.execute.before blocks the tool and the text reaches the model; session.idle -> client.session.promptAsync starts a new turn; promptAsync accepts model/agent/system/tools/noReply; the event hook is not awaited. Claude 2.1.296: sends server/discover before initialize; protocol 2025-11-25; capabilities roots and elicitation, no sampling; _meta carries only toolUseId and progressToken. Wrong or outdated in ddflow: Cursor stop can continue (followup_message, loop_limit 5) and subagents take a model; Windsurf is Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI is a separate surface; Antigravity is three surfaces and 2.17 moved its config; Copilot has autopilot and agentStop block; Codex has spawn_agent with model and effort; Claude instructions cap is 4096; Goose Stop can block (inject=[] wrong); OpenHands has MCP; Continue is frozen; Roo is archived; the kilo delta's 'no loop primitive' is wrong. Not possible anywhere researched: sampling; a quota feed for Gemini/Grok/Cursor/Copilot; Cascade stop-continue and session-start
```

## What does ddflow do when an upgrade runs or a new coding agent connects, regarding that agent's onboarding, and how does an agent or the whole project get offboarded?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** ddflow neither verifies nor repairs a new agent's onboarding at connect or upgrade (it only checks the hooks of agents that have hook writers, and proposes on a version difference), has no set of enabled agents (adopt writes for all 22 descriptors by default), keeps no manifest of what it wrote outside marked blocks, and has no offboarding command at all; hooks uninstall removes two hook kinds only
- **Mechanism.** adopt --agents defaults to all descriptors; upgrade_plan emits hooks:missing:<agent>:<name> only for hook specs that exist (claude, gemini); D-upgrade-on-mcp-connect acts on a ddflow VERSION difference, not on a new client; clientInfo/harness detection (B-hx-identity, B-hy-first-call) and the generic onboarding per descriptor (B-hx-onboard-generic) are queued, but verify, redo, manifest and offboard are not; managed markdown blocks carry markers (removable) while JSON/TOML keys, hook entries and plugin files have no ownership record
- **Falsifier.** an existing command or tool removes everything ddflow wrote for one agent, or records which files and keys onboarding wrote

**Probe:**

```console
$ ddflow adopt --help; ddflow hooks --help / uninstall --help; ddflow hooks status; grep upgrade_plan hooks:missing logic; search of the queue for offboard / uninstall / new agent detection / manifest; ddflow --help command list
adopt --agents default: all 22; hooks uninstall: --claude, --gemini, --harness (other agents' writers 'arrive later'); ddflow hooks status lists claude/gemini only; no 'harness', 'offboard' or 'agents' command in ddflow --help; no task mentions offboarding; B-hx-onboard-generic, B-hx-identity, B-hy-first-call, B-hx-cli, B-hx-conformance open; adopt.py tracks only stamped markdown blocks (LEGACY_BEGIN/BLOCK markers, .local-edits), no manifest of JSON/TOML/hook/plugin writes
```

## How can ddflow watch every session for context exhaustion and quota, step the model and effort down at 40/60/80% of the allowance, pick a cheaper model per task by predicted complexity, and reuse what is already queued?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Almost every part exists as a plan or a pattern but nothing joins them: D-quotas pauses at 80% (6 tasks open, meters and enforcement unbuilt), there is no context-fill meter and no 40%/60% ladder, the tier hint is manual and advisory, subagent routing (P-subagents) is by name not by cost, and handoff, restart and transfer (P-agent-memory, P-session-context, P-resume) are queued separately. One pure decision function (the adaptive-flow controller pattern) fed by sampled meters, acting only at safe points through those existing pieces, delivers the goal without a daemon and without a second pause path
- **Mechanism.** meters: Claude Code statusline stdin carries rate_limits.five_hour/seven_day used_percentage and resets_at (R-usage-quota); context size is the last assistant usage in the transcript (the reader B-am-ingest builds, deduped on message.id+requestId); a running interactive session cannot switch its own model, but a dispatched subagent can (the Agent tool takes model:, per the Claude Code driver delta) and a restarted session can start on another model with a handoff; core/flowcontrol.py already has Threshold low/high/critical marks, hysteresis, cooldown, and samples taken at doors with no daemon
- **Falsifier.** an agent exposes neither context nor quota to a hook, statusline or transcript, or a lower tier fails ddflow's gates so often that escalation costs more than it saves (the backtest on 861 completed tasks with ledgers shows tier fit cannot be predicted better than always-balanced)

**Probe:**

```console
$ ddflow search for quota/tier/subagent/context work; list tasks of BL-quotas, P-subagents, P-session-context, P-resume, P-agent-memory, P-agent-compat, B-hot-files; read D-quotas, B-quota-meters, B-quota-pause, B-gap-spend, B-sub-route, the Model-tier hint README section, claude.toml, claude-code delta, services/quota.py, compaction.py, core/flowcontrol.py
BL-quotas: B-quota-profiles done, 6 open (surfaces, docs, loop, pause, discovery, meters); B-gap-spend (usage ledger, per-item budget) open; P-subagents 14 open incl. B-sub-model, B-sub-route (route by name/family), B-sub-metrics (cost, rework); P-agent-memory B-am-handoff/B-am-restart-brief/B-am-ingest; P-session-context B-sc-transfer; P-resume B-res-session-lifecycle; tier hint shipped, advisory only (tier:fast|balanced|deep, manual); claude.toml records no statusline/context/quota/effort facts (three-valued: NOT VERIFIED); implement-phase driver tells the harness it MAY map tier to a model; flowcontrol Threshold(low/high/critical) reusable; no component computes context fill or a 40/60 step-down; B-hot-files overlaps P-change-surface (lease-edit-only-hold)
```

## Where does a feature's change surface leak into shared files, big files and aggregator lists, and what would shrink it?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** A feature's cost is dominated by shared, regenerated or aggregator files rather than its own code: the README, golden snapshots and transcripts, central registries and 35 files over 600 lines; these, not the plugin architecture, cause overlap refusals, stale pins and slow reading
- **Mechanism.** Work is lease-claimed by file glob, so any file many features must edit (README.md is the only shared_glob; snapshot and transcript pins are not) serializes parallel agents or breaks the build when regenerated by hand; aggregator lists (27 notes.extend lines in health.py, REGISTER_ORDER, exemptions.py, gates/__init__.py, mcp.py) need a line per feature; modules of 1,600 to 3,400 lines cost an LLM tens of thousands of tokens to read and hold one lease for unrelated changes
- **Falsifier.** merges touching a hot shared file are a small share, or a typical feature touches only its own module and test

## Is it worth rewriting ddflow's workflow/ETL engines as plugins behind a standard interface managed by pluggy (or another light tool)?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** No for a rewrite: pluggy would add a third runtime dependency and an entry-point scan (~48 ms of a 0.65 s start) and give the in-tree seams nothing they lack, while the real gaps are (a) seven different in-tree registration idioms and (b) no safe path at all for a third party to add a source, sink, gate or reviewer without editing ddflow
- **Mechanism.** extension today is by in-tree change: export kinds auto-discovered from kind_*.py, ticks registered with lazy 'pkg.mod:attr' targets, search sources by register(), gate kinds, harness TOML descriptors, command descriptors in surfaces/declared, event HANDLERS dicts in the fold, config sections by module list. The fold (core handlers) must stay closed: a plugin that changes how the log folds breaks replay and the compat contract. Plugins that run code in the server process also execute whatever a cloned project's config names, which ddflow's trust fencing exists to prevent
- **Falsifier.** a seam that needs hook ordering, wrappers or first-result semantics and cannot be expressed with the existing registries, or a user needing an in-process third-party plugin that an out-of-process command cannot serve

**Probe:**

```console
$ python -c time of importlib.metadata.entry_points(); import pluggy; time ddflow --version x3; python -X importtime -c 'import ddflow.surfaces.cli'; pyproject dependencies; grep of registration idioms (register(, kind_*.py discovery, HANDLERS, ticks target strings, harness TOML, SECTION_MODULES)
entry_points() scan 48 ms; pluggy import 3.9 ms (1.6.0, present only as pytest's dependency, not a ddflow dependency); ddflow --version 0.65 s three times; importing the CLI already costs 517 ms, ddflow.api 470 ms; pyproject: runtime deps are exactly jinja2 and tomlkit by decision D-unify (1), optional extras go through one adapter with a stdlib fallback; mcp_protocol.py notes 'never importlib.metadata: installed metadata is stale in a source tree'; 7 distinct idioms found
```

## Can a finished IMPORTED phase be closed with the importer's own event, without running the phase gate pipeline, so the "finished but still open" nag stops?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED** · item `fix-import-leaves-finished-phases-open`

- **Claim.** A phase the importer created whose every task is done or abandoned can be finished by writing the importer's own `item.completed {"kind": "phase", "imported": true, "evidence": ...}` event, with no phase pipeline; and that write is what stops the brief's "finished but still open" nag.
- **Mechanism.** The nag is `core.schedule.unpickable`, which skips any phase that is `terminal`; the fold sets state=DONE (and completion_evidence) from `item.completed` whatever the item kind, and the importer already writes exactly that event for source-finished work -- so the same event from an explicit command yields the same state without the pipeline.
- **Falsifier.** After the command the phase is still open, or the nag still fires, or the write changes something it should not (a task's state, or a phase the importer did not create).

**Probe:**

```console
$ `uv run pytest tests/test_phase_close_imported.py -q` against main (no verb, no tool) and in the worktree; plus the brief line before and after the command.
On main: 7 failed -- the CLI is `invalid choice: 'close'` and the MCP tool is `unknown tool 'ddflow_phase_close' ... Did you mean 'ddflow_phase_add'?`. With the fix: 9 passed, and the guards (declared commands, help, MCP parity, tool budget, tiers, golden tools/list, import suites) 207 passed. `brief` prints "finished but still open" before the command and does not after; the tasks under it keep their state.
```

## Which record kinds can be edited, noted, linked, removed and reopened, on which surface?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** The record-surface contract (D-record-surface-contract-r2) covers definition records (rules, decisions, goals); the operational kinds bug, lesson, research, memory, task and phase have uneven verbs and uneven CLI/MCP parity: a bug can be found, fixed, invalidated, reopened and listed, but not edited, noted on itself, linked beyond an add-time extends, or removed; reopen and list are CLI-only
- **Mechanism.** each kind has its own handlers and command code (surfaces/commands/*, api/*), so a verb added to one kind does not reach the others; only rule has edit/remove/show on both surfaces
- **Falsifier.** a bug, lesson, research note or memory can be edited or annotated through an existing command or tool

bug: found, file-tasks, fixed, invalid, reopen, list (MCP: bug_found, bug_fixed, bug_invalid, bug_file_tasks: no reopen); lesson: add, verify, search, list (MCP: add, search, verify); research: add, list (MCP: research_add); memory: add, list, forget; rule: add, edit, list, search, show, remove, sync (MCP has all); decision: add, list, show, search, applicable, supersede; task/phase: add, list, plus update/remove/split by id; 'a record cannot point at itself': a closed or own record cannot be annotated, only another open record can be extended
```

## Can ddflow give each coding agent (claude, kilo, cursor...) its own parallelism cap under one global cap, with slots that are booked on demand, kept alive, and freed automatically when the agent dies?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Today there is ONE cap over all live leases, an agent is only a name, a slot exists only as a task lease, and a dead agent frees its slot only by lease expiry (ttl 1800s + grace 120s); per-agent caps, slot booking ahead of a task and per-agent visibility do not exist
- **Mechanism.** services/flowstate.in_flight counts state.active_leases (every holder, no grouping); core/flowcontrol adapts one limit from host signals; leases.py gives ttl/heartbeat/expiry judged lazily on read (no daemon); infra/harness_identity records the harness per process but not as an attribute of the lease; [schedule].resources already books named capacity per claim but by hand
- **Falsifier.** an existing knob or tool bounds in-flight work per agent or per harness, or lets a pipeline hold capacity without an item lease

**Probe:**

```console
$ grep -rn 'max_parallel_tasks' ddflow (only schedule/flowstate/flowcontrol use one global number); sed flowstate.in_flight (sums active leases of every holder); ddflow config --explain --filter schedule (no per-agent key); ddflow mcp tool list (no slot tool)
in_flight(state,cfg,now) = count of active leases with no holder or harness filter; schedule knobs: parallel, max_parallel_tasks/min/max, adapt_*, signals, ready_policy... none per agent; lease.ttl_s=1800 heartbeat_s=300 grace_s=120; active_leases already drops expired leases, so a dead agent's slot is released after ttl+grace without a daemon, but its worktree stays (reclaim_policy=report)
```

## Why does upgrade --apply leave acknowledged config items in the plan?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED** · item `fix-upgrade-plan-never-empties`

- **Claim.** A partial apply (a refused item keeps the stamp at the old version) records settled item ids in upgrade.applied, but plan.build derives items only from the stamp baseline and never subtracts them, so acknowledged items return every time and apply re-acknowledges them
- **Mechanism.** build() = config_items(changes since baseline); baseline = last upgrade 'to' which a partial apply leaves unchanged
- **Falsifier.** go(old,'all') then plan(old) no longer lists the acknowledged ids, and a second apply acknowledges nothing

## Is the partial-apply stamp marker 0.0.0 a version, and can it be reported as "predates stamps" without hiding the leftover upgrade items?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED** · item `fix-B439c42848f`

- **Claim.** The partial-apply marker `0.0.0` is not a version: reporting it as "predates stamps" keeps --plan consistent with --check, and does not make the partial apply's leftover items look done (the fallback to the stamp this very write adds is what the marker prevents).
- **Mechanism.** `project_version` reads the last upgrade's `to`. A partial apply records `to = frm or UNSTAMPED`, so `0.0.0` means "not brought up, and there was no stamp to keep". `version_key("0.0.0")` parses, so the old code returned it and surfaces printed it. Returning "" for the marker (and NOT falling through to the `ddflow_versions` scan, which now holds the stamp this very write added) yields the same plan contents as 0.0.0 did -- `_wanted`/`instruction_items` treat "" and "0.0.0" alike: `not baseline` and `is_older("0.0.0", running)` are both true.
- **Falsifier.** After a partial apply on an unstamped project the plan reports up-to-date (or project_version == running), i.e. the leftover items stop being news.

**Probe:**

```console
$ uv run pytest tests/test_upgrade_apply.py -k "marker_as_a_version or partial_apply" with `is_stamp` reverted to `bool(version_key(version))`, then with the fix; plus the whole upgrade family.
Unfixed logic: test_a_partial_apply_does_not_present_its_marker_as_a_version FAILS with `AssertionError: 0.0.0` (assert '0.0.0' == ''), 1 failed / 2 passed. With the fix: 121 passed across tests/test_upgrade_apply.py + test_upgrade_plan.py + test_upgrade_stamp.py in 124.63s (including test_a_partial_apply_leaves_the_rest_of_the_plan asserting project_version != running, and the plan still listing the pending config items).
```

## Where does the test suite's time go, and why 78 min on GitHub CI against 6 min locally at -n 48?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Locally the suite costs 245 cpu-minutes spread as a flat tail (3,276 tests over 1 s carry 91% of time), with a real python -m ddflow subprocess (0.6 s cold start) per run_cli call over 4,635 call sites; at 4 vCPU that cpu total is at least 61 min, consistent with 78 min on CI (the runner itself was not measured)
- **Mechanism.** cpu-seconds / vCPU: 14,700 / 4 = 61 min before runner slowdown
- **Falsifier.** A CI run with --durations that shows wall time not scaling with cpu (io or network bound), or per-test time on the runner far from 4x the local figure

**Probe:**

```console
$ uv run --with pytest-xdist pytest tests/ -q -n 48 --durations=0 -p no:cacheprovider in a detached worktree; static grep of run_cli sites; timed git init fixture and ddflow --version
MEASURED 2026-10-12 on main 9b382909, 192-core box, `pytest tests/ -q -n 48 --durations=0`: 11480 passed, 1 skipped, 413.6 s wall; user 210.7 min + sys 34.4 min = about 14,700 cpu-seconds. Sum of reported setup+call+teardown 13,691 s (call 11,178, setup 2,507 = 18%, teardown 6). Time is a flat tail, not a few offenders: top 10 tests 509 s (4%), top 60 1,695 s (12%), top 200 3,342 s (24%), top 1000 7,463 s (55%); 3,276 tests took >=1 s (under -n 48 load) and carry 12,525 s (91%), the other 7,895 tests 1,166 s. Slowest: test_the_loop_cli_transcript_is_unchanged 110.8 s (fix-loop-transcript-slow), test_cadence_phase_close 50.8 s plus five 40-42 s siblings (file total 258 s), test_upgrade_dry_run three SETUPS of 47 s each (file 243 s), test_uc_surf_knowledge_pin 37.6 s, test_lines 35 s x2, test_companions_verify 32 s + 30 s, test_uc_surf_registry_rule_transcript 32 s, test_addenda_render 31 s, test_cli brief budget 29 s, test_remedy_texts 28.7 s x2. Slowest files by summed time: test_api_layer 446 s, test_flow 326, test_cadence_phase_close 258, test_upgrade_dry_run 243, test_lines 214, test_shard_high_water 205, test_cli 176, test_merge_queue 166, test_generated_views 161, test_add_dedupe_cli 149. Static counts: 7,277 test functions (11,480 with parametrize) in 597 files; 4,635 run_cli( call sites in 378 files (each a real `python -m ddflow` subprocess); 534 other subprocess/Popen/check_* sites; about 2,918 test signatures take the `repo` fixture (8 git subprocesses each, 0.05 s alone). Single-process probe: `ddflow --version` 0.615 s, `ddflow status` 0.679 s wall (cold start; matches R-perf-profile-2026-10-11 0.53 s import cost): 4,635 call sites x 0.65 s = about 50 cpu-minutes if each ran once, and many sit in loops, so the subprocess start floor is the dominant cost class (B-perf-lazy-cli attacks the floor itself; fix-test-duration-cut removes the calls). CAUSE OF 78 MIN ON CI: the suite is cpu-bound (user+sys 245 cpu-min). ubuntu-latest has 4 vCPU: 14,700 cpu-s / 4 = 61 min at perfect scaling, plus slower shared cores, cold uv cache, and 3 matrix legs competing is a 78-min wall; this machine's 192 cores at -n 48 give 413 s. So local 6 min vs CI 78 min is the core count (about 12x in cpu, 4 vs 48 workers) and not a different test set. NOT MEASURED: the CI runner itself, the 47:30 vs 1:17:46 variance (cause unknown: runner load or the tests added between), `-n auto` vs loadscope/worksteal on 4 cores. Subprocess counts above are static call sites, not dynamic invocations.
```

**Sources:** tests/conftest.py repo and run_cli; .github/workflows/ci.yml; R-perf-profile-2026-10-11

## Is a rewrite of ddflow (whole, or a native hot core) in Rust or Go worth it, and what would justify it (2026-10-11)?

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** Not now. The measured cost is algorithmic and avoidable inside Python (asdict deep copies, 3-6 folds per command, full-log reads for a Lamport max and a dedupe check, eager import of the whole CLI): fixing them is small, keeps 7,258+ tests and the event format, and is worth ~2.5-6x on the hot commands before any native code. A native fold/parse core (PyO3) pays only when the log passes ~500k events (fold+read ~27 s CPU, 1.3 GB RSS in Python), which at 4.1k events/day is ~4-5 months out and which snapshots/coalescing (B-gap-log-scale) push out by a factor of 5-10. A full rewrite is not justified: the hot core is ~13.5k of 110.7k source lines (12%); 36% of the lines are services/ that are I/O and policy.
- **Mechanism.** wc -l of ddflow/ (110,731 lines, 393 files; core 8,807, core/handlers 1,945, infra 7,793 (log.py 1,802, store.py 983), services 40,913, api 12,696, surfaces 4,987, config_sections 2,635); tests 129,183 lines / 611 files / 7,258 test functions. Compiled-parse proxies measured: orjson/msgspec 2.7-2.9x over json.loads (0.36 -> 0.12-0.13 s per 56k events); DuckDB read_json (multithreaded C++) ~0.25 s for the 779 MB / 1.13M-event log per pass vs 6.9 s Python; Python interpreter start 15-40 ms and import of the CLI 0.25-0.55 s are the non-algorithmic floor a native single binary would remove for hooks (a Rust/Go binary starts in ~1-5 ms: THEORETICAL, not measured here). Effort and risk figures are estimates (THEORETICAL).
- **Falsifier.** A profile where the fold's cost remains dominated by interpreter overhead after asdict and repeated folds are removed at 56k events, or an event log above 500k events within the next quarter.

**Probe:**

```console
$ Arithmetic from R-perf-profile-2026-10-11 and R-perf-duckdb-measured; estimates: cheap Python fixes 1-2 weeks of lane time; PyO3 fold core ~4-6 weeks (handlers 1,945 + model 401 + records + upcasters, JSON-equal State output proven by replay-equivalence over this log) plus wheels per platform (maturin, 6-8 targets) and a pure-Python fallback that must stay bit-identical; Rust/Go hook binary ~3-4 weeks and a second implementation of the redactor, Lamport allocation, shard format, flock protocol and upgrade stamps; full rewrite 6-12 months and every one of the 22 harness descriptors, the 112 MCP tools, upcasters and 7k+ tests reimplemented.
Thresholds that would justify native code (proposed, to be configured as budgets): (a) hook p50 (SessionStart / UserPromptSubmit / heartbeat) over 300 ms idle after the Python fixes -> a Rust or Go fast path for the hook subset only (append + Lamport high-water + redaction); (b) fold+read of the shared log over 3 s idle after snapshots/checkpoints at the expected size -> PyO3 core; (c) steady-state RSS of a resident MCP server over 1 GB -> same; (d) more than 1M events in an active log. None is met today after the cheap fixes are applied; (a) and (b) are met TODAY without them (hook prompt 1.27 s, status 3-5 s under load; idle likely half).
```

**Sources:** R-perf-profile-2026-10-11, R-perf-duckdb-measured, R-gaps-evidence, D-no-duckdb, D-compat

## Where does ddflow spend its time on its own real repository (56.5k events, 38.7 MB, 238 shards), per command, hook and the MCP server (2026-10-11)?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** Wall time is CPU-bound Python in the log read + fold, repeated several times per command, plus an eager import of the whole CLI; git subprocesses (0-23 per command) and I/O are not material. Three cheap defects dominate: (1) dataclasses.asdict in records._claim, called three times per lease.renewed during every fold, is 42% of a profiled fold and ~25-60% of command time; (2) one command folds the log 3x (status, load/leases scan/status) and the SessionStart hook and MCP initialize fold 5-6x; (3) every append computes the highest Lamport by loading the parsed snapshot of ALL 240 shards (~0.4 s at 56k events) before writing one line, and the UserPromptSubmit hook then also read_all()s for its double-fire check. Extends R-perf-100k and the read-snapshot record Rb9e3498a92.
- **Mechanism.** cProfile (-m cProfile -m ddflow), -X importtime, git shim on PATH logging each git invocation, os.wait4 rusage for cpu time, A/B interleaved runs. Scratch clone, never the live store.
- **Falsifier.** status CPU time under 1 s at 56k events, or asdict absent from the fold profile.

**Probe:**

```console
$ [REDACTED:path] not used; scripts in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-delian-src-ddflow--claude-worktrees-bridge-cse-015NbhRCT5XtidHYRvkjBCLK/e0567917-2370-56c0-a094-caf440a8b983/scratchpad/perf/{cmdbench,prof.sh,ab,scale,gen,contend,mcpbench,analytics,parse}.py; repo = clone of main at c7b92799 with its committed events. Load average 32-300 on 192 cores: python -c pass = 38 ms here (about 15 ms idle), so absolute numbers are inflated ~1.5-2x; ratios and shares are the evidence. Medians of 5.
CPU seconds, median of 5 (wall == cpu, i.e. no waiting): ddflow --version 0.58 (python bare 0.04; import of ddflow.surfaces.cli 0.53; -X importtime: ddflow.api 0.56 s of 0.62 s total, jinja2 0.04, ddflow.config 0.07); brief --item 4.9 (6 git calls); next 2.7 (3 git); status 4.9 (3 git; one run 3.2); gate status 1.5 (4); show 1.9 (3); board 2.8 (3); recall 2.8 (3); search 5.3 (3); doctor 7.8 (23 git); render 3.8; rebuild 3.9 (1 git); replay 3.0; heartbeat 2.8 / 4.3; task add 3.5 (1); claim 6.2 (11 git); release 3.8 (6); hooks prompt 1.27 (2 git); hooks session-start 6.0 (10 git). MCP server: spawn->initialize reply 9.1 s (5 folds, 12 s of 25 s profile in fill_queue for the instructions), tools/list 13 ms but 112 tools = 100,012 bytes (~25k tokens per session), then every call re-folds: ddflow_status 4.2 then 3.4 s, next 1.4, brief 3.6, recall 1.9, show 0.8; resident RSS 255 MB. cProfile status (15.3 s profiled): fold x3 = 9.1 s; _h_lease_renewed 7.1 s; asdict 6.4 s (233,949 calls, 6.6M _asdict_inner); graph.closure 3.3 s; progress.detect 3.0 s; plan_for 1.5 s. Session-start (29 s profiled): 6 folds 19.2 s, asdict 13.8 s, store.ensure (index rebuild) 5.5 s, worktree drift 4.8 s. Prompt hook (1.7 s profiled): import of ddflow.surfaces.cli 0.67, read_all 0.68 (240 shards x snapshot seed), append 0.2. First append in a fresh process: 365-389 ms (log._highest_lamport 0.49 s profiled: 240 x _load_snapshot, marshal.loads of every shard), second append 55-134 ms. Prototype in a scratch copy (NOT production): replacing asdict(lease) by a dict copy: status 5.17 -> 3.93 s cpu (-24%, A/B interleaved x7), fold alone 0.68 -> 0.28 s; plus folding once per process (memo): status 8.29 -> 5.11 s in a noisier A/B pair (ratio 0.62 vs base). Scaling (fold+read CPU, DDFLOW_SNAPSHOT=0, 1 process): 56.5k events 0.8-1.1 s read + 0.7-1.0 s fold, RSS 155 MB; 113k 2.0 + 2.4 s, 277 MB; 565k 13.8 + 13.8 s, 1.3 GB; 1.13M 27 + 17 s, 2.6 GB (linear, ~2.3 KB RSS and ~45 us CPU per event; the existing read snapshot gave 1.5x at 56k and no measurable gain at >=113k in my harness - a symlinked events dir, possibly a harness artefact, not verified). Real log grows ~4.1k events and 2.7 MB per active day (R-gaps-evidence). Append contention (N processes x 40 appends, empty log, global flock): 1 proc 0.3 ms p50; 4: 1.9 ms; 16: p50 2.8 ms, p95 255 ms, max 1.4 s; 64: p50 69 ms, p95 2.0 s, max 9.8 s, 114 appends/s overall.
```

## What do the DuckDB primary docs and the installed wheel say about extensions, file format, concurrency, vector search, size, licence (2026-10-11)?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** DuckDB 1.5.6: the Python wheel statically links core_functions, icu, json, parquet only; fts and vss are NOT bundled and need INSTALL from the extension repository (network; fts 11.6 MB, vss 32.9 MB downloaded; works with a pre-seeded extension_directory offline). FTS index does not update automatically when the table changes; BM25 only; docs mention no phrase/prefix/trigram. Storage: newer reads older since v0.10, older reading newer is best-effort, migration is EXPORT/IMPORT DATABASE (so a derived index would need rebuild-on-version-change; harmless for a derived cache). Concurrency: one read-write process, or many read-only processes; no multi-process writers (Quack remote protocol beta). HNSW persistence needs an experimental flag because WAL recovery is not implemented for custom indexes. Licence MIT. Wheels: linux x86_64 21.6 MB, aarch64 19.5, macOS arm64 15.5, win amd64 13.2; installed _duckdb .so 58 MB.
- **Mechanism.** Read duckdb.org docs pages (full_text_search, internals/storage, connect/concurrency, vss) via fetch and summarised by a small model: wording quoted below is the fetch tool's quotation, not read by eye on the page; wheel facts measured: duckdb_extensions() in the installed 1.5.6 wheel, LOAD fts offline failed with 'Extension fts not found', INSTALL fts then LOAD succeeded in 0.45 s, PyPI JSON for wheel sizes, dist-info METADATA for licence.
- **Falsifier.** fts present as STATICALLY_LINKED in duckdb_extensions() of a stock wheel.

**Probe:**

```console
$ venv: uv pip install duckdb (1.5.6); duckdb_extensions(); LOAD fts with default extension_directory; pages: https://duckdb.org/docs/current/core_extensions/full_text_search , /internals/storage , /connect/concurrency , /core_extensions/vss ; https://pypi.org/pypi/duckdb/1.5.6/json

## Does DuckDB beat SQLite FTS5 for ddflow's search/recall index, cold start, memory and analytics on the real data (2026-10-11)?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED**

- **Claim.** No for the index: on 3,129 real records (and 11,380 doc/code chunks) SQLite FTS5 is 10-60x faster per query, 10x cheaper to cold-start (19 ms vs 220 ms in-process, 13.5 MB vs 66 MB RSS), has phrase/prefix/trigram that DuckDB FTS lacks, and its index updates incrementally. DuckDB wins only on scan analytics over raw jsonl at 500k+ events (1.3 s vs 6.9 s at 1.13M events) and on vector scan at 30k+ vectors; neither is a bottleneck at ddflow's 56k events / 3k records.
- **Mechanism.** Same texts (3,129 records from the real index.db: lessons, decisions, research, bugs, prompts, items, memories; 11,380 chunks of repo docs/code) loaded into SQLite FTS5 (porter+unicode61, plus trigram) and DuckDB 1.5.6 FTS (porter, english stopwords). DuckDB FTS needs INSTALL fts from the network (not in the wheel), the index is a static snapshot (not updated on insert), and it has no phrase/prefix/trigram. Per-query medians over 20 reps x 15 lexical queries (+5 phrase, 5 prefix, 5 substring, 4 regex).
- **Falsifier.** DuckDB lexical query p50 under SQLite's, or cold start under 50 ms, on the same corpus.

**Probe:**

```console
$ Scripts (not in the repo): /tmp/claude-1001/-home-delian-src-ddflow--claude-worktrees-bridge-cse-015NbhRCT5XtidHYRvkjBCLK/e0567917-2370-56c0-a094-caf440a8b983/scratchpad/perf/{mkcorpus,build,query,cold,analytics,vec,gen}.py; venv /tmp/claude-1001/-home-delian-src-ddflow--claude-worktrees-bridge-cse-015NbhRCT5XtidHYRvkjBCLK/e0567917-2370-56c0-a094-caf440a8b983/scratchpad/perf/venv (uv pip install duckdb==1.5.6). Machine load average 30-300 on 192 cores during all runs: numbers are medians of 5-20 repetitions and inflated 1.5-2x vs idle; ratios are the evidence, not absolutes.
Cold process, query+open (n=9 median): sqlite 19 ms in-process / 78 ms process wall / 13.5 MB RSS; duckdb 222 ms / 364 ms / 66 MB (threads=2: 204 ms / 76.5 MB). import sqlite3 6-7 ms; import duckdb 128-172 ms (-X importtime). Build, records (3,129 docs, n=5 medians): sqlite porter+trigram 2.2 s (porter only 0.37 s), 22.5 MB (porter-only 7.8 MB), RSS 21 MB; duckdb bulk read_json + FTS 1.54 s (FTS index 1.25 s), 6.6 MB, RSS 106 MB. Row-by-row executemany into DuckDB: 3.6-20 s for 3,129 rows (anti-pattern, avoid). Build, docs (11,380 chunks): sqlite 3.8 s/94.7 MB (porter-only 0.5 s/34.5 MB), duckdb 2.5 s/20.5 MB, RSS 177 MB vs 39 MB. Query p50 in-process (records / docs): lexical OR-BM25 sqlite 1.5/5.3 ms vs duckdb 24.9/33.0 ms; phrase 0.13/0.25 vs 14.7/17.0 (duckdb ILIKE scan, FTS has no phrase); prefix 0.11/0.29 vs 5.8/14.8 (regex scan); substring/trigram 0.25/0.73 vs 3.8/5.8 (contains scan); regex 2.4/10.6 vs 3.0/6.7 ms (duckdb native RE2 wins on docs; sqlite uses a Python REGEXP). Production fused porter+trigram ranking: 5.6 / 13.1 ms p50. Ranking overlap@5 over 15 real ddflow queries, DuckDB BM25 vs SQLite FTS5 BM25: 0.83 (records) / 0.84 (docs), top-1 identical 12/15; vs ddflow's fused ranking 0.81 / 0.77 (differences: stopword list, OR semantics, BM25 variant). Analytics over the real jsonl (56,551 events, 38.7 MB; events/agent/day + gate failure rate + item.started->completed median in one pass): python json.loads+Counter 0.40 s vs duckdb read_json x3 scans 0.27 s (0.21 at 4 threads), 0.07 s on a loaded table; synthetic 10x (565k events, 389 MB): 3.6 s vs 0.88 s; 20x (1.13M events, 779 MB): 6.9 s vs 1.3 s, duckdb RSS 3.0 GB at 20x. Vector cosine top-5, 384-d random vectors: 3,000: python+sqlite blob 98 ms vs duckdb array_cosine_similarity 41 ms; 30,000: 574 ms vs 38 ms. Compiled-parse proxy for the log: json.loads 0.356 s vs orjson 0.133 s vs msgspec 0.121 s per 56.5k events (565k: 3.37/1.38/1.26 s).
```

## Why does run_shell with 1 MiB stdin time out on 3.12.3?

**Verdict: CONFIRMED** · item `fix-B-proc-stdin-resume`

**Verdict: THEORETICAL**

- **Claim.** They are worth building as configuration and shipped templates on existing engines (document types, gate defs, schedule jobs, def-records, reviewer dispatch), each off or advisory by default so no existing project changes behaviour: the skills' own evidence is that agents rewrite historical records, verify a noun not a verb, and skip gates under pressure, which ddflow already answers with enforced rules for gates but not for documents or scenario tests.
- **Mechanism.** The skills encode failure modes (rewriting dated specs, a clean stamp over unverified claims, pasted review output treated as a request, stale binaries under test) that ddflow's log, gates and cross-family rule can detect mechanically if the data exists: a class per document, a reviewed sha plus deferred count, a card with falsifiers, a lens per gate.
